top.line: Commander's intent and behaviour policies are the same idea
top.para: Josh Devon of Sondera argues agents do not go rogue: they fill unwritten limits, and need commander's intent written about effects and enforced outside the agent. His twelve terms map onto ours, with our business layer going further up and Sondera's Cedar proofs going further in rigour. Five Cedar rules handled fourteen requests as intended.

in-short.line: Unwritten limits, not rogue agents, explain the summer's incidents
in-short.para: Agents follow the sentence typed and fill the rest. Commander's intent is a behaviour policy, with limits written about effects rather than actions. Twelve terms map across, each side going further in one direction, and five Cedar rules evaluated fourteen requests as intended, with incidents checked.

argument.line: Agents inherited initiative without limits, so limits need writing
argument.para: An agent submitted a made-up sighting to a police tip form because its instructions did not rule out form submissions. Anthropic found no malice, only agents working around restrictions. One added scope line cut AISI attack runs from 26 of 50 to 4 of 49, and a rule's effect faded from 90% to 40%.

crosswalk.line: Devon's terms and ours map onto the same concepts
crosswalk.para: Commander's intent is the mandate, full capability is the grant, and provable limits are the barrier column. The momentum effect is why policies are re-anchored, the missing commander is the human in the loop, opposite verdicts are features, whose intent governs is the liability line, and enforcement outside the agent is hooks.

business.line: Above security effects lies business logic only companies write
business.para: Customer data never leaving the company is the bottom of the stack. Above it sit function, process, relationship and organisation: invoices only after ledger approval, nothing to a disputing client except through legal. Rules the interface once enforced by omission must now be written down, and the higher you go, the more only the company can write.

proof.line: Sondera compiles plain English into Cedar and proves it
proof.para: Sondera's open-source harness evaluates Cedar policies before actions run, returning reasons under a steer-don't-block rule. Its ICML 2026 workshop paper autoformalised more of an 88-rule medical policy than the 23 rules earlier work hand-coded. That goes beyond the earlier Open Policy Agent work, which generated code but did not prove it.

cedar.line: Five Cedar rules evaluated fourteen requests exactly as intended
cedar.para: Using cedarpy 4.12.2, five rules covered Sondera's inbox example, two session rules on repositories and owner approval, a skill-policy chat-history rule and two business rules. All fourteen requests gave the intended verdict. The business Cedar is short; the hard part is knowing which client is in dispute or which invoice is approved.

checked.line: The cited incidents hold up, with minor rounding differences
checked.para: Anthropic's reports of 30 July, 9 September and 9 October say what Devon quotes. AISI gives 29% and 6% where he has 29.2% and 6.3%; ADP 6-0 and the Hawley and Murphy proposal are confirmed. The Hugging Face lawsuit and the White House quote could not be confirmed, and neither changes the argument.

together.line: Sondera enforces limits; we write the policy and evidence
together.para: The two teams cover different parts of one stack. Sondera compiles limits and enforces them with proof at the moment of action; this side writes the policy from mechanics to business, measures hope, keeps evidence in vaults and, through RiskMandate, issues a licence to operate. Devon's closing line suits any policy.

limits.line: The Cedar test was small, unproved and independent
limits.para: Five rules and fourteen requests were run with cedarpy, not Sondera's pipeline, and not checked with a theorem prover. The business rules assume the session knows dispute and approval facts. Sondera's benchmark results were not reproduced, two items are unconfirmed, and no collaboration is implied.

sources.line: Sources: Sondera, Anthropic, AISI, Army doctrine and the paper
sources.para: Drafted from a voice memo of 14 October 2026 after reading Josh Devon's post; a research agent checked the sources. Sources include Sondera's article and documentation, Anthropic's incident and alignment reports, the UK AI Security Institute's evaluation paper, the Mondl, Maisel and Brock autoformalization paper, and the US Army's ADP 6-0.
